books.section: Topic 7.3 The Spanish-American War and Its Aftermath

primary_sources: President William McKinley, message to Congress, April 11, 1898

stimulus.source_note: President William McKinley, message to Congress, April 11, 1898, public domain (abridged).
stimulus.text: "First. In the cause of humanity and to put an end to the barbarities, bloodshed, starvation, and horrible miseries now existing there, and which the parties to the conflict are either unable or unwilling to stop or mitigate. It is no answer to say this is all in another country, belonging to another nation, and is therefore none of our business. It is specially our duty, for it is right at our door. Second. We owe it to our citizens in Cuba to afford them that protection and indemnity for life and property which no government there can or will afford. . . . Third. The right to intervene may be justified by the very serious injury to the commerce, trade, and business of our people, and by the wanton destruction of property and devastation of the island." — President William McKinley, message to Congress, April 11, 1898 (abridged)

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim abridged excerpt from President William McKinley, message to Congress, April 11, 1898, public domain
stem: A historian arguing that McKinley's message was written to persuade a reluctant Congress would point to the fact that the message

options.text: Asks Congress to declare war on the Philippines
options.misconception: The message asks Congress to authorize measures in Cuba; the Philippines are not its subject.

options.text: Blames the Maine explosion on Spain and its agents in Havana
options.misconception: The passage never mentions the Maine, let alone blames Spain for it.
McKinley promises nothing of the kind; Congress itself later disclaimed annexation in the Teller Amendment.

options.text: Lists different kinds of reasons, so members could each find one convincing

rationales.A: The message is about Cuba. Background: the Philippines enter the story only after Dewey's victory at Manila Bay.
rationales.B: The Maine goes unmentioned here. McKinley builds his case on Cuban suffering, citizens, and trade.
rationales.C: McKinley asks for measures to end the war in Cuba. Annexation is not promised anywhere in the message.
rationales.D: Humanity, citizens, trade: three different appeals in one list, each aimed at a different doubt in Congress.
rationales.general:
1. Remember the audience. McKinley is asking Congress to authorize force, and Congress has been divided.
2. Count the appeals. Humanity speaks to the humanitarians, citizens to the cautious, trade to the business-minded.
3. See the design. One reason would not have been enough; the list is built to gather votes.
Remember: a list of reasons is a coalition in words, so ask which audience each reason is meant to win.
